Chinese robotics company Unitree has unveiled the As2-W, a new wheel-legged robot that combines the speed of wheels with the flexibility of four legs. It automatically switches between driving and walking depending on the terrain. It can reach speeds of 21.6 km/h, travel over 30 km on a single charge, climb 45° slopes, clear 80 cm obstacles and handle stairs, gravel and other rough terrain. It’s also water and dust resistant and can operate in temperatures from -20°C to 55°C.  Unitree says it’s designed for everything from industrial inspections and cargo transport to research and outdoor exploration, making it a bridge between consumer and professional robotics.  #unitree #robotdog #robot #futuretech #chinatech

XPENG’s humanoid robot, known as IRON, represents the company’s expansion beyond electric vehicles into robotics and embodied AI. XPENG, a Chinese EV manufacturer founded in 2014, has leveraged its expertise in electric drivetrains, AI software, and autonomous systems to develop robotic platforms capable of dynamic movement and real-time environmental interaction. Humanoid robots like IRON rely on advanced motion planning algorithms, electric actuators, and sensor fusion systems - typically combining cameras, LiDAR, inertial measurement units (IMUs), and force sensors. These systems allow the robot to maintain balance, adjust posture, and perform coordinated movements that appear fluid and human-like. Modern humanoid locomotion depends heavily on real-time feedback control. Small positional corrections are made hundreds of times per second to stabilize joints and prevent falls. This is similar to the control architecture used in self-balancing robots and autonomous vehicles. XPENG’s broader robotics initiative aligns with a global push toward general-purpose humanoid platforms - machines designed to operate in human environments rather than factory-only settings. While still in early development stages, such robots are being researched for applications ranging from logistics and manufacturing to service roles and human-robot interaction studies. I spent days teaching a 3D-printed robot duck to walk. Most of that time, it was falling over. It’s my own build of the Open Duck Mini. The open-source, BDX-inspired biped created by Antoine Pirrone. The whole thing is 3D-printed and runs on hobby-grade servos instead of industrial actuators, which is what makes it buildable on a normal budget and also what makes it so hard to get walking. The hard part wasn’t the printing or the assembly. It was the sim-to-real gap. A gait that walks perfectly in MuJoCo hits real-world joint slop, servo lag, and a center of mass that won’t sit still, and just before you know it, the duck face plants into the floor. It took me 40+ calibration passes before it could take three steps without tipping! What the build came down to: • 3D-printed chassis • Per-joint offset calibration (where most of the pain lived) • Policy training in simulation (MuJoCo / Isaac Lab) • Build guide + docs via Tnkr • A lot of failed walks Real hardware. Real failures. Real progress.

Industrial humanoid robots are looking less humanlike every day.  The Chinese company LimX Dynamics just shared footage of its TRON 2 dual-arm robot integrated with an industrial robotic arm. The TRON 2 multi-form-factor robot has gone viral in the past for its modular design that can transform into a humanoid, a quadruped, or even be combined into a centaur.    In the industrial setup, TRON 2 is mounted onto a traditional robotic arm to extend its reach. It uses a custom attachment to hold and operate a power drill and nailer to assemble wooden frames and panels. It then applies spray finishing.    The TRON 2 is priced starting around $7,000 in China but international pricing begins around $13,000.   Shenzhen-based LimX is scaling production of its TRON platform, along with its full-sized humanoid robot Oli, and its sister, Luna, after securing around $400 million so far in 2026. Valued at $2.2 billion, it's one of many Chinese robotics startups racing toward a public listing. #robotics #robot #industrialrobot #ai #automation

I'm sorry... but who looked at this and said, "Yep, that's the design!"? 🤣 If your rescue robot walks out of the woods looking like a seven-foot-tall mechanical demon carrying a chainsaw... maybe the branding department got a little carried away. 😂 They could have made it look like a normal industrial robot. Instead they named the company after a satyress (a mythical goat-like creature), gave it giant ram's horns, painted it matte black, and then acted surprised when the internet said, "What in the horror movie is THAT?" 😆 Sure, the company says the shape protects sensors and helps it work in dangerous environments. But let's be honest... the dramatic mythological look is also part of the branding. It gets people talking—and judging by all of us arguing about it, it worked. 😄 If I ever need rescuing in the woods and this thing comes walking toward me with glowing eyes... my first thought isn't going to be, "Thank goodness!" It's going to be, "Well... this is one interesting way to meet my maker." 🤣👹🤖
